_about: Hard Hat Mack, Electronic Arts, 1983. A 42,112-byte .COM with no compiler
prologue anywhere in it, so probelib.py finds nothing -- 0 of 250 entry
points, a real negative result. It is still machine-generated: `mov al, 0
/ inc al / dec al` appears hundreds of times to set flags after a load,
and `cmc` follows almost every `cmp`. That is why there are 221 call
targets for perhaps eighty distinct behaviours.
All of them are named here, and the whole code region was read to do it.
The variables live next to the routines that own them -- 436 addresses in
132 clusters scattered through the image -- and the two that carry most of
the traffic are Mack's block at 0x0B60 (391 references in 0x21 bytes) and
Five names in the previous version were wrong, all of them guessed from
caller counts. The worst was `shift_history`: it is the routine that saves
the tune position so a sound effect can borrow the speaker. The game has
no sound hardware beyond one bit, and it plays music by running a phase
accumulator against a drifting duty threshold -- pulse-width modulation,
_not_addresses: Six bracketed constants in the listing are not addresses at all:
0x001E, 0x0047, 0x0302, 0x0601, 0x2402 and 0x5F7F. Each sits inside a run
of table bytes that comrec classified as code because it decodes cleanly --
its two neighbours, and 0x04952. NASM re-emits them as the same bytes, so
the rebuild is unaffected, but `and bx, word [0x1e]` is a coincidence of
the encoding and naming 0x001E would invent a variable the game does not
This is the mirror of the residue problem knowledge/11 records. There the
question was whether unreached bytes are code; here it is whether reached
bytes that decode are data. Both are answered by what refers to them, and
